title: The ideal trial: defining causal estimands that balance relevance and feasibility in target trial emulations and actual randomized trials
extended_summary:
This paper is a methodological/conceptual article about causal inference, not an education or ChatGPT intervention study. It addresses how researchers should define the causal estimand of interest when conducting either randomized trials or observational studies that emulate a target trial. The central argument is that investigators should begin from an "ideal trial"—a hypothetical perfectly designed randomized experiment—and then explicitly consider how actual trials or observational target trial emulations depart from that ideal.

The paper does not test an educational intervention, does not involve ChatGPT, and does not report any student writing or motivation outcomes. Instead, it uses a respiratory epidemiology example based on exclusive breastfeeding and childhood asthma to illustrate the distinctions among an ideal trial, a partially aligned target trial, and an observational emulation using the HealthNuts cohort. The example is used only for methodological illustration, with formal discussion of causal estimands, intention-to-treat versus per-protocol effects, selection bias, missing data, measurement error, and generalizability.

The population discussed in the worked example is neonates born in Melbourne who can be breastfed, with later follow-up to asthma outcomes at age 6. The context is epidemiologic methods, not schooling or educational technology. The authors conclude that specifying a target trial solely to align with available observational data can obscure important biases relative to the estimand of real practical interest. They recommend that researchers explicitly define the ideal trial and then describe how target trial emulations or actual randomized trials differ from it, so that all relevant assumptions and bias sources are transparent.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a methodological/theoretical epidemiology paper about causal estimands, ideal trials, and target trial emulation. It does not evaluate any educational AI intervention, does not report a ChatGPT writing experiment, and provides no empirical education outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational intervention effect estimated in this paper, so it provides no usable impact evidence for ChatGPT-based writing feedback or student motivation/writing outcomes.
